entities.summary:
Theodoric II of Moers (1385–1463) emerged as a formidable Prince-Archbishop of Cologne from 1414 until his death, a pivotal figure who navigated the tumultuous ecclesiastical and political landscape of the Holy Roman Empire during the late Medieval period. His tenure was marked by an ambitious expansion of archiepiscopal temporal power, often at the expense of secular princes and free imperial cities, fundamentally shaping the regional balance of power in the Lower Rhenish-Westphalian Circle. He became one of the most powerful and controversial prince-archbishops of his era, a testament to the enduring struggle between spiritual authority and territorial ambition within the fragmented empire.

His archiepiscopacy was characterized by relentless political maneuvering and military engagement. Theodoric II was a prominent participant in the Council of Basel (1431–1449), initially advocating for conciliar supremacy before shifting his allegiance to Pope Eugene IV, a strategic move to secure papal support for his territorial claims. His most significant and costly conflict was the Soest Feud (1444–1449), a protracted struggle against the city of Soest, which sought to free itself from archiepiscopal overlordship and align with the Duke of Cleves. Despite his eventual military victory, the conflict drained the archdiocese's finances, leaving it heavily indebted and impacting his successors for decades.
